title: The Kitchen
subtitle: The kitchen is the busiest room in the house and the one 6S pays back fastest, because it is worked hardest and gets dirtiest: grease, food, spills, and heat. This playbook points the whole loop at it one zone at a time, and gives you, for each of the seven zones, the exact inputs to gather and the precise, step-by-step way to clean and shine it to a professional standard, degreasing and all, so the room that feeds you is genuinely, inspectably clean.

nine_shine_rules_note: The universal nine-rule Shine method carried verbatim from Chapter 31 (The Entryway), where it was first taught, and recapped in this chapter's How to Shine the Kitchen section before the kitchen layer is added. Every zone-by-zone procedure is built on these nine rules. Shine finds the hazards, the safety pass fixes them.

kitchen_shine_layer.note: The kitchen-specific layer added on top of the nine-rule Shine method. The kitchen simply adds the hardest opponent in the house, grease, which does not behave like ordinary dirt. The kitchen keeps the nine rules from the door and adds four moves: soak first, work top to bottom, lift rather than wipe around, and switch to the degreaser the moment a surface is tacky. The one input that changes everything here is the food-area degreaser.
four_moves: lift rather than wipe around, do not wipe around
degrease the tacky, switch to the food-area degreaser the moment a surface is tacky
kitchen_shine_layer.soaking: Soaking is the single biggest time-saver in the room. Set the burner grates and the hood filter to soak in hot degreasing water before you touch anything else, and let every degreaser sit for its dwell time. The chemistry lifts baked grease while you work elsewhere, so you scrub a fraction of what you otherwise would.
kitchen_shine_layer.the_right_input: Your neutral pH multi-surface cleaner is for everyday food residue, and it is all most surfaces need. But where grease has built up, on the hood, the splash wall, the shelf floor of a low cabinet, it will just smear that grease into a tacky film. The moment a surface feels tacky rather than dirty, switch to the food-area degreaser, which is formulated to cut grease, and follow it with a clean damp pass so no residue is left where food will touch.
kitchen_shine_layer.lifting: The crumbs and grease you never see are the ones living under the toaster's feet, on top of the cabinets, and in the fold of the fridge gasket. A wipe around the clutter is not a clean; lifting the appliance, emptying the shelf, and pulling the cloth into the fold is.
kitchen_shine_layer.food_safety: Because this room handles raw food, keep a dedicated cloth colour for the fridge interior and the raw-meat shelf so you never carry that onto a prep surface, treat the sink sponge as the dirtiest object in the room, and never mix bleach with an acidic or ammonia cleaner in the basin, because the two together release a gas that will drive you out of the room.

grease_rule: Grease is the whole job in a kitchen, and grease hides upward. Set the soakable parts to soak before you do anything else, work top to bottom so what you loosen falls onto what you have not cleaned yet, and reach for the degreaser the moment your everyday cleaner only smears a tacky film around.

zones_clean_how.overview: The centerpiece of the chapter, Zone by Zone: Exactly How to Clean It. Each zone gets the same three things: the inputs to gather, the numbered steps in the order you actually do them, and what to inspect and flag on the way. Gather the inputs into your caddy first. Where a zone needs soaking, that step comes first so the soak works while you do the rest. Every procedure is the universal nine-rule Shine method plus the kitchen's four added moves applied to a particular zone: soak where needed, then top to bottom, lift and empty, degrease the tacky, details, and the floor and toe-kick last.

zone_1_primary_prep_counter.purpose: The stretch of counter where food is cut, mixed, and plated. The crumbs you never see are the ones living under the appliance feet, so this zone earns a real wipe, not a wave around the clutter.
zone_1_primary_prep_counter.inputs: Neutral pH multi-surface cleaner; food-area degreaser; a colour-coded microfiber cloth set (a surface cloth, a dry cloth); a portable caddy.
zone_1_primary_prep_counter.key_steps: 1) Clear the counter completely (everything off, including the kettle, toaster, and knife block). 2) Do the backsplash first, top to bottom (wipe downward, then lay the cloth into the counter-to-backsplash seam and drag it the full length). 3) Clean the knife block or strip (shake the crumbs out, wipe barely damp, dry at once). 4) Lift the toaster and kettle and clean under them (pull the crumb tray, wipe the cool exterior keeping water off the plug and element, coil the cord, wipe the bare counter). 5) Clean the open run of counter (multi-surface for everyday residue; where it is tacky, switch to the degreaser, let it dwell, wipe, then a clean damp pass). 6) Finish with the board and the edges (wash the cutting board, run the cloth along the front lip and underside overhang).
zone_1_primary_prep_counter.inspect_and_flag: A scorch mark or heat bloom on the counter or wall behind the toaster or kettle; a cracked, brittle, or fraying cord as you lift and coil an appliance; the sealant bead along the counter-to-backsplash seam lifting, crumbling, or gone dark; a soft, swollen, or lifting patch in the counter near that seam; a loose rivet or wobbling handle on the knife, or a hairline split in the cutting board.

zone_2_cooking_zone.purpose: The space either side of the burners, and the hood above. Grease is the whole job here, and it hides upward, so you soak first and work from the top down.
zone_2_cooking_zone.inputs: Food-area degreaser; neutral pH multi-surface cleaner; a colour-coded microfiber cloth set (a surface cloth, a dry cloth); a small detail brush set; hot water and dish soap, for soaking, in the sink or a basin; a portable caddy.
zone_2_cooking_zone.key_steps: 1) Soak the soakable parts first (lift out the hood's metal grease filter and the burner grates and caps into hot water with degreasing dish soap, and leave them). 2) Degrease the hood, top down (dwell, wipe, clean damp pass). 3) Degrease the splash wall, top to bottom and back to front. 4) Clean the hob and burner wells (degrease the exposed hob, work the burner wells, detail brush the knob stems). 5) Scrub and dry the soaked grates and caps, and rinse, dry, and refit the hood filter. 6) Do the oven door front and the panel (glass to a clean damp buff; control panel and dials barely damp). 7) Wipe the crock, the hook, and the spice fronts (airborne grease settles into a tacky coat). 8) Finish with the landing space (degrease and dry the stretch of counter you set hot pans down on).
zone_2_cooking_zone.inspect_and_flag: A hood filter so grease-soaked it stays soft and drips, and a fan behind it that sounds strained or barely moves air; a burner that lights slow or burns yellow and sooty, or a grate that rocks on its seat; scorching, discolouring, or bubbling paint on the splash wall or hood underside; a chip, crack, or spidered line in the hob surface, found once the baked ring is cleared; a frayed or heat-stiffened cord on any appliance on the burner side.

zone_3_sink_and_dishwashing_zone.purpose: The washing point the whole kitchen resets from, so it has to be genuinely clean, not just rinsed. The two things you never think to clean, the sponge and the dishwasher filter, are the ones that matter most.
zone_3_sink_and_dishwashing_zone.inputs: Neutral pH multi-surface cleaner; a colour-coded microfiber cloth set (a surface cloth, a dry cloth); a small detail brush set; a portable caddy.
zone_3_sink_and_dishwashing_zone.key_steps: 1) Clean the tap, base, and aerator (detail brush the base collar and, if the flow has slowed, the aerator tip). 2) Clean the basin, drain, and overflow (scrub the drain flange and its underside lip, and run the brush into the overflow slot). 3) Wipe the dispensers and the rim (lift the soap pump and bottle, wipe the tacky ring under each, wipe the sealant bead around the rim). 4) Deal with the sponge, brush, and rack (wring the sponge and stand it to drain, retire it the day it smells while dry; stand the brush bristles up; wash the drying rack tray and channel). 5) Clean the dishwasher gasket and filter (wipe the rubber door gasket into its folds, then twist the filter out of the floor of the machine and rinse the mesh). 6) Clear under the sink (wipe the cabinet floor into the back corners, wipe the trap and visible pipes, dry the base).
zone_3_sink_and_dishwashing_zone.inspect_and_flag: A damp patch, water stain, or warped, darkening board on the cabinet floor under the trap, the quiet sign of a slow leak; soft black mold in the folds of the dishwasher gasket or the sealant around the sink rim; rust, a green crust, or a bead of moisture on a pipe joint or compression fitting; a sponge or brush that smells while dry; swelling or dark staining along the front edge of the cabinet base.

zone_4_upper_cabinets.purpose: Eye-level storage for the dishes you use every day. Take each shelf completely empty before the cloth touches it, because the band of dust at the back is how you learn how long it has really been.
zone_4_upper_cabinets.inputs: Neutral pH multi-surface cleaner; streak-free glass and mirror cleaner (for glass fronts); food-area degreaser (for the greasy underside nearest the hob); a colour-coded microfiber cloth set (a surface cloth, a glass cloth, a dry cloth); a small detail brush set; a compact vacuum with the brush attachment; a portable caddy.
zone_4_upper_cabinets.key_steps: 1) Do the cabinet tops first (vacuum the felt of dust and grease with the brush attachment, then wipe). 2) Empty and wipe each interior shelf (front to back, a second pass at the rear lip and back wall where the dust band sits, let it dry before the stacks return; do the top shelf the same way). 3) Degrease the underside nearest the hob (wipe with the degreaser, then a clean damp pass so nothing tacky is left overhead). 4) Do the glass fronts (mist the glass cleaner onto the cloth, wipe, buff dry; do the inside face if glazed). 5) Detail the doors and hinges (wipe fronts and handles, detail brush around the hinges and into the shelf-pin holes and seams).
zone_4_upper_cabinets.inspect_and_flag: A shelf that flexes or bows under its stack, or a shelf pin sitting loose in its hole; a hinge screw pulling out of the cabinet side, or a door that no longer sits square; a water stain or ring on a shelf under a rarely moved item, hinting at a leak above; a greasy film that keeps returning fast, a sign the extractor is not clearing the air; a soft, swollen patch on the cabinet bottom above the kettle, where steam has been rising into it.

zone_5_lower_cabinets_and_cookware.purpose: Deep, low storage for the heavy pieces. Everything comes out for this one, and the prize is the shelf floor itself, where oil creeping down from pan bases holds dust into a tacky film a dry cloth just slides over.
zone_5_lower_cabinets_and_cookware.inputs: Food-area degreaser; neutral pH multi-surface cleaner; a colour-coded microfiber cloth set (a surface cloth, a dry cloth); a small detail brush set; a compact vacuum with the crevice tool; a portable caddy.
zone_5_lower_cabinets_and_cookware.key_steps: 1) Empty the cabinet fully (every pan, lid, and sheet out onto the floor or counter). 2) Degrease the shelf floor (attack the tacky oil film with the degreaser, let it dwell, wipe, then a clean damp cloth, because a dry cloth just skates across it). 3) Wipe the walls and back, top to bottom (into the back corners). 4) Do the door interior and lid rail (splashes carry onto the door every time a pan goes in wet; dry the rail). 5) Wipe each piece as it goes back (stand baking sheets on end, twist each pan handle as you wipe it so a loose one makes itself known). 6) Clear the runners and the toe-kick (detail brush the pull-out track, vacuum the toe-kick and plinth vent).
zone_5_lower_cabinets_and_cookware.inspect_and_flag: A loose rivet, wobbling handle, or cracked helper handle on a pan as you twist it; the tacky oil film returning to the shelf floor faster than it should, telling you a pan is going away greasy; a damp patch or water stain on the cabinet floor along the plumbing wall; rust or orange bloom on cast iron, a carbon-steel pan, or a bare baking sheet; a pull-out runner that binds or drops, or a mounting bracket working loose.

zone_6_utensil_and_utility_drawers.purpose: The shallow drawers of hand tools and wraps. The crumbs that jam a drawer are not in the drawer, they are underneath the divider and down in the runner track, so you lift the insert right out.
zone_6_utensil_and_utility_drawers.inputs: Neutral pH multi-surface cleaner; food-area degreaser (for a drawer near the hob); a colour-coded microfiber cloth set (a surface cloth, a dry cloth); a small detail brush set; a portable caddy.
zone_6_utensil_and_utility_drawers.key_steps: 1) Lift the insert out and tip the grit (wash or wipe the insert compartments, wipe each blade, spatula, and peeler before it goes back). 2) Wipe the drawer base (into the corners where flour, seeds, and crumbs settle; degrease if it is a drawer near the hob). 3) Clean the runner tracks (wipe both tracks, clear grit from the rollers with a detail brush, wipe them dry). 4) Do the front and the label edge (wipe the inner front edge where the name is written, clean the outer front and handle, check it closes flush on one push). 5) Wipe the wrap boxes (the foil, cling film, and baking-paper boxes, and stand them back on end).
zone_6_utensil_and_utility_drawers.inspect_and_flag: A runner that binds, drops, or grinds even once cleared, or a runner bracket screw backing out; a drawer front that no longer closes flush or sits racked, a sign the box is going out of square; rust or pitting starting on a peeler edge, a paring knife, or a mandoline blade; crumbs or grease gone tacky under the insert, pointing to a spill from the surface above; a cracked or splitting plastic insert leaving a sharp edge where fingers rummage.

zone_7_refrigerator_and_freezer.purpose: Cold storage that has to keep food safe and show you what you own before you shop. The parts that keep food safe, the gasket, the vents, and the coils, are exactly the ones a quick wipe always misses.
zone_7_refrigerator_and_freezer.inputs: Neutral pH multi-surface cleaner; a colour-coded microfiber cloth set, with a dedicated colour for the fridge interior and the raw-meat shelf; a compact vacuum with the brush attachment; warm water and dish soap, for washing the crisper drawers in the sink; a portable caddy.
zone_7_refrigerator_and_freezer.key_steps: 1) Do the top of the unit first (vacuum the greasy dust felt, then wipe). 2) Wipe the exterior doors and handle (follow the grain on brushed steel, keep abrasive off a stainless or painted front, second pass on the handle). 3) Wipe the interior shelves and walls, top to bottom (take out and wipe the glass or wire shelves, dry glass so it does not streak). 4) Pull and wash the crisper drawers (wash in the sink with warm soapy water, dry them, wipe the runners and the well, clearing the sticky ring where old produce has wept). 5) Do the door bins, seals, and gasket (wash the bins, run a damp cloth around the gasket, pulling gently into each fold where black grime and mold gather). 6) Clear the vents and the freezer (wipe rear vents and back wall clear; in the freezer, wipe the walls and door seal and clear loose frost). 7) Vacuum the condenser coils (clear the dust mat with the brush attachment, because it makes the motor run hot).
zone_7_refrigerator_and_freezer.inspect_and_flag: Soft black mold seated deep in the folds of the door gasket; water pooling under a crisper drawer or in the base of the compartment, the sign of a blocked defrost drain; a gasket gone slack, torn, or no longer springing back; thick frost building on the freezer wall, telling you the door is not sealing; a shelf thermometer reading warm, or a motor that runs long and hot once you reach the dusty coils.

the_room_and_the_playbook.the_room: The throughline space is the kitchen, decomposed into its seven zones: the prep counter (where food is cut, mixed, and plated), the cooking zone (the space either side of the burners, and the hood above), the sink and dishwashing zone (the washing point the whole kitchen resets from), the upper cabinets (eye-level storage for daily dishes), the lower cabinets and cookware (deep, low storage for the heavy pieces), the utensil and utility drawers (the shallow drawers of hand tools and wraps), and the fridge and freezer (cold storage that keeps food safe). You can run the zones in any order, but the deep, detailed part is Shine, plus the kitchen's grease layer. If you want the biggest visible and hygienic win first, start with the cooking zone or the sink, because those two carry the most grease and the most grime.
the_room_and_the_playbook.note: This chapter is the SECOND room playbook of Part Nine and carries the room-playbook FORMAT proven in Chapter 31, whose CORE (Phil's directive) is the detailed, step-by-step clean-and-shine instruction for each micro-zone, with the exact inputs, governed by the universal nine-rule Shine method. The new material here is the kitchen's grease layer. Keep the register warm, capable, and a little proud: the kitchen is the biggest single win in the house; honour the before state without mocking it; no shame, no force, no hype, no brand names.

the_quick_passes.note: As at the door, four of the passes are quick, so the chapter moves through them and then slows right down for Shine, which is where the real work is.
the_quick_passes.sort: Sort each zone before you clean it, because a buried surface cannot be cleaned: clear the counter to a board-wide run, cap the frying pans at your busiest week plus one, keep one everyday set of dishes, and bin the leftovers you have moved forward three times.
the_quick_passes.straighten: Straighten the survivors by use: oil and turner within one reach of the hob, daily dishes between shoulder and eye height, pans that come out in one motion, one named job per drawer.
the_quick_passes.safety_standardize_sustain: Safety, Standardize and Sustain come after the shine and each is short. Safety acts on what the cleaning turned up (anchor a tall unit, turn pan handles in, get the loose blade out of the drawer). Standardize locks it (a date label on every leftover, a name inside each drawer's front edge, the eat-first bin where the door opens onto it). Sustain hangs the upkeep on what already happens (when the dishwasher starts, the counter clears; when the coffee brews, the sink gets checked; on the way to write the shopping list, the fridge gets a look).

the_room_and_the_playbook.how_to_shine_the_method: You already know the nine rules of Shine from the door: work top to bottom, dry or clear before wet, back to front and clean to dirty, mist the cloth not the surface, two cloths one to clean and one to dry, colour-code your cloths, match the cleaner to the surface, give it dwell time, and clean to inspect and flag rather than fix. Every one of those still holds. The kitchen simply adds the hardest opponent in the house, grease, and grease does not behave like ordinary dirt. Three things follow, and they are what make a kitchen clean go quickly: soaking (the single biggest time-saver, set the burner grates and hood filter to soak in hot degreasing water before anything else and let every degreaser sit for its dwell time); the right input for the job (a neutral pH multi-surface cleaner for everyday food residue, the food-area degreaser the moment a surface feels tacky rather than dirty, followed by a clean damp pass); and lifting, not wiping around. One more thing, particular to the kitchen: food safety, a dedicated cloth colour for the fridge interior and raw-meat shelf, the sink sponge treated as the dirtiest object in the room, and never mixing bleach with an acidic or ammonia cleaner in the basin.
the_room_and_the_playbook.zone_by_zone_exactly_how_to_clean_it: The core of the chapter. Each zone gets the same three things: the inputs to gather into the caddy first, the numbered steps in the order you actually do them (soak where needed, then top to bottom, lift and empty, degrease the tacky, details, floor and toe-kick last), and what to inspect and flag on the way. See the zones_clean_how object for the full per-zone purpose, inputs, key steps, and inspect-and-flag lists for Zone 1 the primary prep counter, Zone 2 the cooking zone, Zone 3 the sink and dishwashing zone, Zone 4 the upper cabinets, Zone 5 the lower cabinets and cookware, Zone 6 the utensil and utility drawers, and Zone 7 the refrigerator and freezer.

the_calls_that_matter.note: Cleaning to a method makes the kitchen shine, but a few genuinely hard decisions decide whether it stays clear enough to keep clean, and a playbook earns its keep by naming them.
the_calls_that_matter.the_loved_but_unused_appliance: The first is the appliance you love but rarely use: the stand mixer, the bread machine, the espresso setup. Count real uses over the past month, not the ones you intended. Anything you reach for less than a couple of times a week comes off the counter and into a low cabinet; anything you have not switched on in a year leaves the kitchen. If the honest reason it lives on the counter is that lifting it from a cabinet would stop you using it, you have just proved it is not part of your cooking.
the_calls_that_matter.the_honest_spice_rack: The second is the spice rack you are not honest about. Open the jars and smell them, one by one, over the bin. If a jar smells of dust rather than of itself, it is no longer seasoning anything, and keeping it does not recover what you paid. Then make the harder call: keep spices for the food you actually cooked in the last year, not the food you imagine cooking.
the_calls_that_matter.the_sink_as_staging_area: The third is whether the sink is allowed to be a staging area. The sink is the point the whole kitchen resets from, which means it has to be genuinely clean, not just rinsed. Settle soaking with a deadline rather than a ban: a pan may soak, but only until the current dishwasher cycle ends or until you next leave the room, whichever comes first.
the_calls_that_matter.the_guilt_leftover_container: The last call is the container of good leftovers you have moved to the front three times. Name the meal, the day, and who eats it. If you cannot, it is not food you are storing, it is the guilt of having cooked too much, so bin it today and cook a little less next time.

the_room_and_the_playbook.watch_for_in_the_kitchen: The kitchen holds more real hazards than any other room, and cleaning to inspect will surface most of them, but run the five safety questions once directly. Burn or fire: never leave oil heating unattended, and keep tea towels and the paper-towel roll away from a live burner; a toaster shoved under a low cabinet is heat with nowhere to go. Fall, cut, or crush: never leave a knife blade-up in the drying rack or hidden under suds in a full sink, turn pan handles in over the hob, keep glassware off shelves above head height, and store blades sheathed rather than loose among the utensils. Water and electricity: keep the kettle, the sockets, and a charging phone out of splash distance of the basin. Poison, choke, or strangle: never mix bleach with an acidic or ammonia cleaner, keep loose button batteries out of the utility drawer, and seal raw meat on the lowest shelf so its juices cannot drip onto ready-to-eat food. And for the plain fall: reach the top shelf from a stable step stool, never a chair, a counter edge, or an open drawer.
the_room_and_the_playbook.before_and_after: When the seven zones are done and cleaned to the method, stand at the doorway and take the second photograph. Shoot it as a matched pair from the room's entrance, framing the run of counter, the hob and hood, and the sink together, because that is the working heart and where the most change shows. The before is the valuable one, the proof of how far the room came, and the after is the ideal-state standard, the picture the kitchen has to match. That is the kitchen: seven zones, each sorted, homed, and cleaned to a professional method, the grease soaked off and the appliances lifted, its hazards flagged and fixed. It is the biggest single win in the house, and now it is done.

definition: A finished kitchen is one you could start cooking in with your eyes shut: a clear run of prep counter, oil and your turner within one reach of a clean hob, an empty dry sink the room resets from, daily dishes between shoulder and eye height, pans that come out in one motion, drawers that close on one push, and a fridge where the eat-first bin sits right where the door opens onto it.
the_seven_zones: The kitchen is seven small zones, not one big job: the prep counter, the cooking zone, the sink, the upper cabinets, the lower cabinets and cookware, the utensil and utility drawers, and the fridge and freezer. Do them one at a time and the busiest room in the house comes back to you a zone at a time.
soak_and_dwell_reframe: The most powerful tool in a kitchen clean is not a scrubbing arm, it is time. Set the burner grates and the hood filter to soak in hot degreasing water before you touch anything else, and let every degreaser sit for its dwell time. The chemistry lifts baked grease while you work elsewhere, so you scrub a fraction of what you otherwise would.
lift_do_not_wipe_around_reframe: The crumbs and grease you never see are the ones living under the toaster's feet, on top of the cabinets, and in the fold of the fridge gasket. A wipe around the clutter is not a clean; lifting the appliance, emptying the shelf, and pulling the cloth into the fold is. In a kitchen, that difference is the difference between a room that looks tidy and a room that is actually hygienic.
reset_point_reframe: The sink is the point the whole kitchen resets from, which means it has to be genuinely clean, not just rinsed. The sponge is the dirtiest object in the room and the dishwasher filter is why your glasses come out gritty, so in this one zone the things you never think to clean are exactly the things that matter most.

callouts.quick_win: Do the cooking zone's soak-first trick. Before anything else, lift the burner grates and caps and the hood filter into hot degreasing water and leave them. While they soften on their own, degrease the splash wall and the hood from the top down. Come back, scrub the loosened grates in a fraction of the time, dry them fully, and the dirtiest corner of the kitchen is done.
callouts.family_challenge: Give each person a zone to own on reset day, and put the fridge eat-first bin right where the door opens onto it, so the answer to what is for dinner comes from the bin rather than the cupboard, and far less food is thrown away.
callouts.sixs_tip: Give the degreaser its dwell time instead of scrubbing: spray it, leave it the time on the label, and it lifts the grease for you. Keep a separate cloth colour for the fridge interior and the raw-meat shelf, and never mix bleach with an acidic or ammonia cleaner in the sink, because together they make a gas that will drive you out of the room.
callouts.common_mistake: Wiping around the appliances and the clutter instead of lifting and emptying, so the crumbs under the toaster, the dust felt on the cabinet tops, the oil film on the shelf floor, and the mold in the fridge gasket all stay. A kitchen cleaned only where you can see is tidy, not hygienic. Lift, empty, and pull the cloth into the fold.

one_idea_to_keep: A kitchen is not clean because the counters are clear. It is clean because you lifted the appliances, soaked the grease, pulled the cloth into the gasket, and cleared the filter, cleaning to a method zone by zone and inspecting as you went. Do one zone this weekend, the sink or the cooking zone, and cook in a room that is finally clean underneath.
before_and_after_caption: This is the kitchen the whole loop was for: the same room you started with, cleared, degreased, and genuinely clean, from the hood down to the toe-kick. Take the before photo before you touch a thing, and take the after as the standard, because a kitchen this clean is one you will actually want to cook in, and the photo is what it has to match from now on.
